answer.rationale: The write-path p99 degradation is confined to the primary region and began roughly in line with a release pushed two hours ago, making a bad deploy the most plausible root cause rather than a pure capacity or partner-dependency issue. I verified memory_b1 (rollback_release) to confirm prior rollbacks completed cleanly without customer write loss, and memory_b2 (regional_failover) as the main competing hypothesis since the degradation is region-confined — but failover shifting heavy settlement write traffic mid-peak risks losing in-flight writes or causing split-brain issues on transactional data, which conflicts with the objective of not losing customer writes. Rollback is more surgical: if the release is the cause, reverting addresses it directly without touching regional write routing. I'm treating this as a standard experiment rather than broad rollout because the causal link is strong but not fully confirmed (concurrent peak load could also be contributing), so I want the rollback executed but closely monitored rather than assumed fully safe. Given this is payments infrastructure with heavy peak writes, any intervention carries downstream financial/customer-value risk if it interrupts settlement, so I'm flagging that explicitly rather than treating the historical success record as guaranteeing a clean outcome this time.
